title: FlakeScope: Ranking Flaky Test Failures
Comments for authors:
The authors propose a system for training large language models on hardware connected over the public internet and distributed around the world. This is a difficult problem (EleutherAI writes that “doing volunteer-driven distributed compute well for this use case is an unsolved problem”) and the authors tackle it with a combination of pipelining and data parallelism.

As this setting can’t assume homogeneous network performance, the parallelism assignment problem is much more difficult than it is in datacenters, and the authors apply a novel combination of algorithmic approaches to solve it, including treating pipelining and data parallelism independently and scheduling parallel units onto workers using an evolutionary algorithm.

The authors report benchmark results on a series of increasingly heterogeneous network configurations, showing significant speedup relative to a grid-search-optimized Megatron setup with homogeneous data and pipeline parallelism.


The authors do a good job of motivating the problem and pointing out weaknesses in existing systems (e.g. a focus on data parallelism or mixture-of-experts models).

The paper uses the terminology “macro-batch” but it’s sometimes unclear whether this refers to the portion of the global batch that runs on one data-parallel replica, or to the portion that runs on one stage of one data-parallel replica (more often called a microbatch). I’d recommend being a little clearer here.

The algorithm the authors introduce seems reasonable and well-motivated. If it’s fast enough, and if decomposing the assignment problem into separate data and pipeline levels isn’t a restrictive assumption (both of these appear to be true!) then it also seems like the only algorithm we need for this problem. (It might be possible to optimize in an even greedier way, but if the evolutionary approach is fast enough I’m not sure it matters).

I’m somewhat disappointed that a system for heterogeneous distributed training (justified in part by a seemingly accurate claim that home electricity is 50-100x cheaper than spot GPU instances) was benchmarked only on cloud machines with cloud networking, not on machines with conventional home internet. But it looks like the bandwidth between distant datacenters in the authors’ experiments is low enough that it might be representative of home network connections.

The authors present good benchmarks against grid-search-optimized Megatron configurations, and their ablations, although brief, are convincing about the value of their local search strategy.


How much do you lose by decomposing the assignment problem into separate data and pipeline levels? I think the answer might be “nothing”, but it would be great to be more explicit about that.

The intra-node bandwidth is quoted as 100 Gb/s in your experiments, but IIUC V100 NVlink is 150 GB/s (1200 Gb/s); is there a reason this isn’t the right number to use for intra-node bandwidth? And in general, are the bandwidths you’re assuming the result of benchmarks? If so, maybe include those benchmarks somewhere?

Were the benchmarks run on cloud machines that were really physically located in different regions, or were the bandwidths between machines limited artificially to simulate inter-region connections?


The authors are clear about most of the limitations of their system, including lack of online failure handling and dynamic replanning.
Comments for PC: A solid paper; I lean towards acceptance.

title: FlakeScope: Ranking Flaky Test Failures
Comments for authors:
This paper presents an interesting result, demonstrating the impossibility of provably efficient batch reinforcement learning (RL) under only two assumptions: a) Realizability and b) Feature Coverage. The authors provide persuasive counter-examples where the state/action space is polynomially dependent on the horizon $H$, yet the sample complexity exhibits an exponential dependence on $H$ with high probability.

However, I have some reservations regarding the Feature Coverage assumption. Unlike the Concentrability assumption [Chen & Jiang (2019), Xie & Jiang (2020a)], Feature Coverage merely postulates that the feature covariance matrix has a minimum eigenvalue of $1/d$. My specific concerns are as follows:
1. Is the Concentrability assumption mathematically more stringent than the Feature Coverage assumption? If so, why is Feature Coverage a primary focus when Chen & Jiang (2019) have already established the necessity of Concentrability for efficient batch RL?
2. Does the Feature Coverage assumption truly capture the notion of exploration within a batch dataset? From an RL perspective, exploration is critical both empirically and theoretically. In the constructed hard instance, crucial states $s_h^*$ are not even within the support of the dataset (which might also violate the Concentrability assumption). While I understand this is necessary to derive the exponential lower bound, it raises questions about the practical representativeness of Feature Coverage for exploratory datasets.
3. Theorem 5.1 is somewhat perplexing. While I grasp that its primary objective is to illustrate Error Amplification, why is an upper bound considered instead of a lower bound? Alternatively, is Section 5's aim to demonstrate that Error Amplification is unavoidable under the Realizability and Feature Coverage assumptions?

In conclusion, I find this paper to be well-written and it effectively addresses its central question under the specified assumptions. I have reviewed the proofs and found no significant errors. While I harbor some doubts about the practical reasonableness of certain assumptions in the context of RL, I maintain a positive outlook on this work. My concerns might be unfounded, and I eagerly anticipate further discussion.

title: FlakeScope: Ranking Flaky Test Failures
Comments for authors:
This paper introduces HALP, a hardware-aware structural pruning method that frames latency-constrained model compression as a global optimization problem. The core idea revolves around combining latency reduction estimates (via lookup tables) with accuracy-aware saliency scores to determine optimal filter pruning strategies under target latency budgets. Experiments demonstrate consistent improvements in throughput across architectures like ResNet-50 and SSD while maintaining competitive accuracy, suggesting practical utility for deployment on edge devices.

The approach’s strength lies in its pragmatic focus on real hardware latency—a metric often overlooked in favor of proxy measures like FLOPs. The integration of saliency scores with latency-aware grouping feels intuitive, and the cross-task validation (classification + detection) adds credibility. However, the paper leaves several breadcrumbs unanswered: While the knapsack formulation is mentioned, the specifics of the "augmented" solver remain opaque. How does it differ from vanilla knapsack approaches used in prior work? Is the solver’s complexity manageable for very large networks, or does it become a bottleneck?

Another curiosity is the treatment of latency predictability. Lookup tables are standard practice, but hardware execution times can be non-linear (e.g., due to memory bottlenecks or parallelization). The paper assumes a linear relationship between pruned filters and latency reduction. Would this hold for architectures with heavy branching or heterogeneous operators? A brief discussion on such edge cases would strengthen the method’s generalizability claims.

The empirical results, while solid, could benefit from more granularity. For instance, the ResNet-50 pruning achieves +0.3% accuracy with 1.6× throughput—impressive, but how does this trade-off curve look at intermediate pruning ratios? Are there "sweet spots" where latency gains plateau while accuracy remains stable? Similarly, the SSD pruning’s 0.56 mAP drop for 1.94× speedup sounds reasonable, but context matters: is this drop concentrated in certain object classes or sizes? A breakdown could inform practitioners about task-specific suitability.

A minor gripe lies in the novelty framing. The global resource allocation perspective isn’t entirely new—prior works like AMC [1] similarly optimize for latency via reinforcement learning. HALP’s differentiation via saliency-weighted knapsack solving isn’t sufficiently contrasted against these alternatives. Is the main advantage computational efficiency during search, or does the formulation inherently capture better trade-offs? Clarifying this would help position the work within the pruning landscape.

Finally, the broader impact claim—"significantly impacting autonomous vehicles"—feels under-supported. While latency reduction is critical for real-time systems, the paper doesn’t validate HALP under dynamic inference scenarios (e.g., varying batch sizes or sensor inputs). Including such experiments, even preliminarily, would better bridge the gap between lab benchmarks and real-world deployment.

Suggestions: (1) Elaborate on the knapsack solver’s mechanics and complexity analysis; (2) Include ablation studies isolating the impact of latency-aware grouping vs. saliency scoring; (3) Discuss hardware-specific limitations (e.g., GPUs vs. NPUs); (4) Compare search time/efficiency against RL-based methods like AMC. Addressing these could elevate HALP from a strong empirical contribution to a more foundational advancement in hardware-aware pruning.

[1] Hu et al., "AMC: AutoML for Model Compression and Acceleration on Mobile Devices," ECCV 2018.
